title: ‘Coffee tax dead in the water’
summary: The proposal to slap an excise tax on coffee in lieu of a higher “sin tax” on alcoholic beverages is “dead in the water,” Marikina 2nd District Rep. Miro Quimbo said yesterday.

blocks.text: Alcoholic drink importers had made the proposal before the House of Representatives yesterday, claiming that so-called sin products have reached tax saturation.
MANILA, Philippines — The proposal to slap an excise tax on coffee in lieu of a higher “sin tax” on alcoholic beverages is “dead in the water,” Marikina 2nd District Rep. Miro Quimbo said yesterday.
They also the change in drinking habits, with Gen Z consumers preferring coffee to alcoholic beverages.
But Quimbo, who chairs the House ways and means committee, noted that an excise tax on coffee would hit the poor, who are the biggest consumers of three-in-one coffee.
While these preparations have been flagged by health experts for their sugar content, he said the mixtures could be reformulated.

Producers of three-in-one coffee can instead be made to gradually reduce the sugar content in the mix, in line with trends in other Southeast Asian countries, he told “Storycon” on One News yesterday.
He also noted that coffee actually does have some benefits to the overall health of a person, citing health experts.

“In fact, some argue that it’s actually healthy. Besides, it’s going to be very difficult to tax considering that there are so many different preparations of coffee. How do you even tax it? Based on caffeine content? Volume? It’s too difficult,” he admitted.
“Let’s not talk or discuss about it first. Let’s take up alcoholic drinks first. Some may even end up sleepy when we discuss coffee,” Quimbo joked.

During the House committee on ways and means hearing led by Quimbo, Olivia Limpe-Aw of the Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines (DSAP) proposed that government divert its efforts to impose taxes on variations of coffee instead.

“There is a changing consumer behavior. Our Generation Z are no longer consuming liquor. They now want coffee. That is why we also want that coffee be taxed as well. That is a huge market – coffee, and it’s very expensive,” she maintained.

The DSAP executive made the proposal after data from the Department of Finance indicated that tax collections from locally manufactured wine were 24.8 percent lower from January to September this year – as compared to the figures in 2025.
The agency also reported a 0.2 percent decline in excise tax collections from locally manufactured fermented liquors.

Albay first district Rep. Krisel Lagman and Bataan first district Rep. Antonio Roman III filed in September a bill imposing a flat excise tax on 3-in-1 coffee as well as flavored fermented milk, citing as basis their high sugar content.

But Finance Undersecretary Karl Adriano acknowledged that, “We learned that our government has been using flavored milk in our nutrition program in schools. That is why we removed flavored milk. While 3-in-1 coffee is also being used by our poorest of the poor.”
